Brilliant paper on agent memory from FAIR at Meta. (bookmark it) A single global history is the usual way to let agents learn from past runs. When tasks are interleaved, it gains almost nothing over no memory at all, an average of +0.015 in normalized reward. This work proposes Routed Continual Learning. Past trajectories are grouped into clusters, and each cluster keeps its state in one memory system from a fixed library. Before each run, an LLM router reuses a cluster or creates a new one. They tested it on a stream mixing 301 CL-Bench instances with 97 banking instances from τ³-Bench, across four language models. Routed CL raised reward over the global history by 15% to 30% of the maximum attainable reward. Estimated API cost fell by 65% to 72%. The runs were sequential, so parallel agents updating one cluster remain untested. If your agents handle mixed work, it might help to split their memory into clusters before adding a bigger memory system. https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.38796 Chat with Paper: https://academy.dair.ai/papers/routed-continual-learning-2610.38796

Banger paper from IBM on decision gates for agents. They add a runtime gate to tool-using agents and keep the models and tools the same. JevAct is a check that sits between the agent and its tools. An LLM first turns the domain policy into code checks and yes/no questions. Before a selected tool call runs, the code checks the facts in the tool records, and a Jev-like decision model answers the questions about the conversation. If the call fails a check, it goes back to the agent with feedback so the agent can revise it. On τ²-bench Telecom, Opus 4.6's success across all three runs rose from 39.5% to 80.7%. On Telecom, all eight agents improved by 16.9 points on average in three-run success. All nine improved on BFCL. Airline results were smaller and mixed. They show that the gains come from the harness. https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.38620 Chat with Paper: https://academy.dair.ai/papers/think-before-you-act-decision-gate-for-llm-agents-2610.38620

Alex Lieberman reveals the problem with selling enterprise AI like software: “there is so much nuance and so much inertia and so many systems you have to wrangle and people you have to wrangle.” “every software company is basically building up a team of FDEs because there’s just this convergence happening of services and software when every company wants all this nuance that was not traditionally expected from software.” “how will they be able to do this at software margins if everyone expects a one-of-one solution?” For software we could simply build it once and sell it multiple times... But with AI, AI buyers want completely custom solutions rather than adapting to software. Every new customer needs custom work, so vendors send FDEs to build bespoke operations. These increase costs, thereby decreasing profit margins... But rather than building each automation completely from scratch, processes can be standardized so that it can quickly be deployed onto multiple enterprises while staying custom. This can simply be implemented by changing the deployment steps: 1) Standardization Consolidate the workflows to complete a task into one process 2) Match Look for companies that do it the same way 3) Build Once Make a single solution that fits the group of companies 4) Tailor Add custom work only for the specific parts that belong to one company This way the deployment for the next customer doesn't start from scratch... The work was already built while the last part may change, it still feels custom but is cheaper and faster to deliver. Media
